#5070. 7 Best Wrinkle Creams of 2026, Tested by Dermatologists and Beauty Editors

Our picks span everything from luxe, high-tech finds to drugstore gems.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Since celebrating a milestone birthday (yay!), I've started to notice a few fine lines and wrinkles that weren't on my face the previous year (ugh!).

Now look, there's nothing wrong with aging gracefully—it's a celebration of a life well-lived—but I'd be lying to your face if I didn't admit that these changes caught me off guard and made me reevaluate my skincare routine. I've tried a few red light therapy devices, and they're helpful—but they're also incredibly pricey. And I'm super-uncomfortable around needles, so injectables like Botox and hyaluronic acid fillers are out of the question—at least for now. The doctors I consulted told me there is no quick fix for aging, but wrinkle creams are a pain-free and surprisingly affordable way to plump unwanted lines. (Our recommendations start at just $22.)

A great wrinkle cream helps hydrate and plump the skin, which ultimately makes fine lines and wrinkles less obvious, so you'll want to start in your 20s when collagen (that's the protein that plumps skin) production slows down. "Prevention is always the best strategy, so consider using a wrinkle cream before wrinkles are especially noticeable," says dermatologist Geeta Yadav, MD. "If you can already see a wrinkle form when you make facial expressions, it may be a good time to integrate a wrinkle cream into your regimen."

Sounds pretty sweet, no? Well, the pros say we'll need to be patient when using wrinkle creams, but the results—and you will see results from the right cream—are worth the wait. You should notice an immediate hydration boost, but wrinkles won't visibly begin to diminish until you've been consistently using your new cream anywhere from 6 to 12 weeks, according to dermatologist Dara Spearman, MD.

Retinol is the holy grail of anti-aging ingredients since it helps stimulate collagen production which results in a plumper, more youthful appearance. SkinMedica has this dermatologist-approved ingredient in spades and unlike other wrinkle creams, you can pick from multiple retinol strengths: 0.25 for beginners, while 0.5 and 1.0 are for the most advanced anti-aging benefits. "Once your skin fully adjusts to retinol, you'll want to try more potent concentrations so you continue to see results," suggests Dr. Yadav.

Beyond retinol, this wrinkle cream is also formulated with SkinMedica's PhytoShield Complex, a proprietary formula of antioxidants that improve skin texture and minimize irritation. To help combat any inflammation your skin may experience, the wrinkle cream's formula also includes magnolia bark extract.

"SkinMedica is a brand I've trusted for years, and their retinol product is, in my opinion, the gold-standard on the market," says Underwood. "I love that it comes in multiple strengths, so you can customize the treatment strength, whether you're a retinol newbie or a seasoned user, like myself."

Underwood says that the formula itself is pretty creamy and moisturizing—a major plus for these types of products—making it a solid choice for normal to dry skin. You'll still need to layer a serum or moisturizer underneath for extra hydration and to prevent potential redness, flaking, and sensitivity. Once your skin becomes used to the low retinol concentration, you can eventually skip the extra step.

"I noticed results from consistent use after about six weeks—and I've been using this product off and on for years," Underwood says. "My horizontal lines have definitely been softened and my skin is glowy and refined. This is worth every cent."

Also, our biggest tip with using this wrinkle cream is to begin twice weekly to avoid any potential flaking or redness typically associated with retinol use, then graduate to nightly use. Apply in the evening after cleansing and toning and before applying your moisturizer.

If you aren't looking to break the bank on a wrinkle cream, Neutrogena's Rapid Repair wrinkle cream is a solid choice, Dr. Yadav says. "I like this product from Neutrogena because it’s a concentrated, yet gentle formula that is also easy to find and has an accessible price point."

In addition to fighting fine lines, wrinkles, and dark spots using retinol (found in many pricier alternatives), the cream is also formulated with hyaluronic acid to hydrate skin, which plumps it up and smoothes the look of lines. Typically, retinol is used at nighttime to avoid irritation, but Neutrogena actually advises using this wrinkle cream twice daily. I was a bit nervous about these instructions, but since my skin is used to retinol and I liberally reapply broad-spectrum sunscreen, I decided to give it a shot.

After slathering on a pearl-sized amount to my freshly cleansed face and neck, I noticed my skin looked more radiant after a few days. With regular use, my smile lines and even some acne-related dark spots also looked less obvious. It also contains similar ingredients to pricer wrinkle creams, including Skinmedica, Dr. Dennis Gross, and Lancôme, but at a fraction of the cost.

One thing to keep in mind is that it isn’t the most cosmetically elegant. Don’t get me wrong. Neutrogena performs well, especially for the price, but I found the cream pills more frequently on my skin than pricier options. That said, as long as I regularly use a face exfoliant then the pilling is relatively minimal.

Caring for sensitive skin can be a real drag since redness, itching, stinging, peeling, and dryness can commonly occur. Thankfully, dermatologist Dr. Dennis Gross, MD, created a sensitive skin-friendly wrinkle cream that's safe for retinol beginners.

How? It's infused with Phyto-Retinol Blend that combines retinol with bakuchiol, rambutan, and ferulic acid to help minimize the retinol uglies that would normally leave skin red and itchy. "That means you get a powerful cocktail of line-minimizing ingredients with pretty much no irritation—a huge plus in my book," says Underwood, who loves this moisturizer because it absorbs into his skin beautifully, leaving it hydrated and plump.

Given Underwood's glowing review and my general love of other Dr. Dennis Gross products, I gave this wrinkle cream a shot. It's a soft, semi-thick cream that spreads across my skin like butter on warm toast. My face is definitely glowing whenever I apply this face cream.

Since I frequently test new beauty products, my skin has become quite reactive. But, I haven't experienced any irritation on my skin since incorporating this epic face cream into my routine. After just two weeks of twice daily use, I noticed my smile lines and hyperpigmentation began to disappear. These spots are normally very stubborn and can take months to vanish, so I was pretty surprised to see speedy results.

That said, you probably won't love this face cream if you're already using a prescription-strength retinoid, like tretinoin, because your skin is used to a quicker exfoliation process. This wrinkle cream combines a super gentle retinol and a plant-based alternative, while prescriptions work much faster but with the risk of irritation. Still, my retinoid–related redness and dryness have practically disappeared since using this soothing face cream, making it a must-have in my routine. I'll continue reaching for this moisturizer when I don’t apply my prescription retinoid cream so my face can still enjoy the hydrating and light brightening effect in the summer without the flakes or itching.

If you're looking for a tried-and-true performer, you've found it here. "Retinol is the most effective over-the-counter wrinkle fighter and RoC is a pioneer in the use of this ingredient," Underwood says. He likes this night treatment because it's a great non-irritating option that's also infused with glycolic acid to minimize the appearance of dark spots.With regular use, you'll notice a more radiant complexion, and deep wrinkles will begin to smooth. It'll take about 12 weeks of daily use before you (and those lucky enough to be around you) will notice visible results. And don't worry about over-exfoliation: RoC contains glycerin and dimethicone for instant skin hydration.

It is important, though, to limit your usage of this product to nighttime only, just as it says on the instructions (you're a rule follower, right?). Because it contains both retinol and glycolic acid—two powerful active ingredients that refine skin texture—this could make your skin extra sun-sensitive if you use it during the day. Sunburns? No thank you. So be sure to slather on your go-to face sunscreen, such as my all-time favorite one from Isdin that helps reverse sun damage.

Olay's Regenerist moisturizer is made with one of the smoothest and creamiest formulas on the list—I love massaging it on. The best part? Hyaluronic acid gives my face instant hydration, which is a welcome year-round treat.

Shea butter is a superstar moisturizer that is like a refreshing glass of water for dry skin and helps maintain dewiness. The antioxidant-rich ingredient helps calm irritation and is even safe for someone with nut allergies because it’s made entirely of fat, according to Cleveland Clinic. Niacinamide, also known as vitamin B-3, helps boost skin cell turnover so skin is extra firm and glowy. Also in there: antioxidants to help fend off the free radical damage caused by air pollution, sun exposure, and smoke that can lead to weaker collagen and cause wrinkles. Free radicals can also cause redness, dryness, and eczema, Dr. Dennis Gross previously told WH.

For me, the rich texture is a winner because it's completely non-greasy, making this formula ideal for dry skin, and surprisingly suitable for my oily skin. Since it's on the thicker side, it'll take a few minutes for my skin to fully absorb the cream, but I don't mind because my face looks and feels noticeably softer. I knew this cream was really working when my friends started asking what I've been using on my face—and swapping in this Olay cream was the only significant change I'd made.

Underwood agrees: "Who says you have to pay a lot for an effective wrinkle cream? Not me," he says. "Olay's classic 'red jar' cream is packed with decades of anti-aging skin science."

The greasy feel of certain skincare products can be unpleasant, but that certainly isn't Lancôme's anti-aging cream. "I often find fancy wrinkle creams to be overly fragranced and far too thick," Underwood says. "That's not the case with this cream, which has a lighter, almost whipped texture that hydrates beautifully without a hint of greasiness."

Like Underwood, I found this wrinkle cream to have a whipped-like texture, and in my experience, it provides ample hydration without congesting my pores. As for the anti-aging benefits, in the short-term I've experienced a more even-toned complexion and my fine lines are less noticeable.

In the long-term Rénergie can help with lower face sagging by using a blend of potent ingredients. "It's a trifecta of active ingredients—moisturizing hyaluronic acid, line-smoothing peptides, and skin-evening niacinamide—handily tackles visible signs of aging with regular use," Underwood says. He recommends making it the last step in your nighttime routine to help prevent moisture loss.

The only downside with this moisturizer is the price. However, the quality of anti-aging superstar ingredients coupled with display-worthy packaging helps justify the added cost. And FWIW, this is the only refillable option on this list. For example, a 1.7-ounce jar of Lancôme’s face cream costs $150, while a same-size refill will only set you back $130. Since each jar is estimated to last two months, you’ll save $100 a year just by purchasing the refills.

"While not typically found in wrinkle creams, daily sun protection is crucial to prevent further wrinkles and skin damage,” says dermatologist Marie Jhin, MD. Since sunscreen is a non-negotiable part of a proper anti-aging skincare routine, Dr. Jhin appreciates the combo of broad-spectrum SPF 30 coverage with hydrating hyaluronic acid and ceramides to keep your skin moisturized and protected.

This CeraVe day cream is also made with encapsulated retinol, a type of non-irritating retinol, to further smooth uneven texture and improve the look of fine lines. The ceramides also help with wrinkle prevention, since they help restore the skin's barrier.

I gotta be completely honest, I didn't love this day cream because it leaves behind a white cast on my complexion, and for that reason alone, it's an automatic return for me. (For reference, I wear shade 9 in Armani Luminous Silk Foundation.) However, if you have a lighter complexion than I do, you should be fine. Here's what I do like: The thicker texture spreads surprisingly well across my face and doesn't pill when layered under my face makeup. It also doesn't make my normally oily skin look like a greasy slice of pizza. Instead, it adds more of a natural-looking luminous glow which is appreciated in the summer.

Also, keep in mind you should apply this wrinkle cream at least 15 minutes before sun exposure and then every two hours for adequate sun protection. So as long as you have the time commitment and a white cast isn't a typical problem you've dealt with, then you're probs a good fit for this wrinkle cream.

The pros I chatted with say the two most important factors to look out for when buying wrinkle creams are your skin type and the active ingredients in the formula. Here are some shopping pointers.

First, you must pair your wrinkle cream with sun protection—up to 90% of visible skin aging is from the sun. "UV exposure from the sun speeds up the aging process by breaking down collagen and elastin, and it can cause pigmentation (such as sun spots and melasma)," says dermatologist Nazanin Saedi, MD.

Retinoids are a class of vitamin A derivatives (like the OTC version, retinol) that are "the single most proven anti-aging ingredients, after sun protection," says dermatologist Hadley King, MD. They boost cell turnover, collagen and elastin, and minimize discoloration, says Dr. King. It's also a fantastic ingredient for treating adult acne and those with oily skin.

Here's the catch: You'll need to start off using a pea-sized amount to avoid irritation, and pregnant women can't use it, says Dr. Spearman. You can also use the sandwich method, which involves adding a base layer of moisturizer, adding the retinol on top, and following up with another layer of moisturizer. Thankfully, there are some very effective retinol alternatives such as plant-based bakuchiol which do a lot of the same great things as retinol, but are safe for pregnant women or those with very sensitive skin, says Dr. Spearman.

Using these proven ingredients isn't enough. "Just as on food labels, ingredients are listed in order of their amounts," says Dr. King. Your safest bet is to use wrinkle creams with the active ingredients listed earlier on in the label instead of at the end for the most effective, anti-aging results. While the order of ingredients does give some information, it's not really enough to know the concentrations unless these are also listed—some brands that pride themselves on transparency do this, but most don't, says Dr. King.

Our skin type also informs our ideal wrinkle cream. For example, those with oily, acne-prone, or combination skin will appreciate a lightweight wrinkle cream, while those with dry skin should look for a richer formula that offers ample hydration. "Heavier creams tend to work better for more mature, more dehydrated skin,” says Dr. Spearman. “These are often too much for those who are acne prone or have oily areas of skin." Generally, brands will list on the box which skin type will benefit from using its creams.

Our team has written about wrinkle creams since September 2023. With endless options on the market (and I mean hundreds!), it can be hard to narrow down what the best options for your skin are. So to help, I chatted with several dermatologists and Women's Health's beauty director Brian Underwood to curate a list of wrinkle creams you'll love adding to your skincare routine.

To ensure we only feature the latest and most effective launches in November 2026, I tested a bunch of wrinkle creams to deliver my unfiltered testing experience to help you determine which one is most ideal for your needs. I carefully researched wrinkle creams aligned with the above expert guidance. As a quick reminder this includes the best ingredients and skin types they’re compatible with. I also considered pricing, each cream’s consistency, how fast they absorb, and the short- and long-term benefits they offer. Additionally, I evaluated how well they layered with other products, like sunscreen and foundation—and nixed anything that pilled.

Ultimately, I tested dozens and settled on the featured picks that earned major snaps from me, my fellow WH editors, and the doctors I consulted.

There are many processes that the body goes through when aging, and one of those is the production of less collagen, which can make your skin more susceptible to wrinkles, Dr. Yadav says. Collagen is what helps the skin maintain its elasticity and resilience.

As you age, cellular turnover also decreases, which causes dead skin cells to build up on the surface of the skin, making its texture look rougher and uneven, and exacerbating the appearance of wrinkles, Dr. Yadav says.

When you opt for wrinkle creams that fight these two things, they can promote stronger, firmer, smoother, and more even-looking skin, Dr. Yadav says. "Additionally, adding moisture into the skin helps to plump up the look of fine lines, albeit temporarily," she adds.

There's really no specific age that's best for working a wrinkle cream into your skincare routine, since people can form wrinkles at different ages depending on their lifestyle, sun exposure, and heredity, Dr. Yadav says.

On the other hand, Dr. Jhin suggests people can start using a wrinkle cream as early as their 20s. "Even though many people start using anti-aging products in their 40s or 50s when signs of aging have become more prominent, your skin’s natural collagen production actually starts to decline around age 25," she says.

Dr. Jhin often tells her patients to think of skincare as a marathon—not a sprint. "There is no 'quick fix' for aging," Dr. Jhin says. "Like regular exercise and a well-rounded diet help you maintain a healthy body, continued, regular use of anti-aging products will help your appearance in the long run."

#5069. Maple Finance’s strategy rift sends co-founder, COO to the exits

Maple Finance co-founder Joe Flanagan and COO Ryan O’Shea are leaving over disagreements about the firm’s direction as SYRUP falls despite revenue growth.

Two senior executives are leaving onchain asset manager Maple Finance over disagreements about the firm’s direction as its SYRUP token slid more than 7% Thursday.

Maple co-founder and executive chairman Joe Flanagan said Wednesday he would leave after seven years at the firm, describing a growing divide with fellow co-founder and CEO Sidney Powell.

“Over time, our views on strategy, leadership, and life have moved further apart,” Flanagan wrote. “I believe Maple is best served by one co-founder leading it forward from here.”

Chief operating officer Ryan O’Shea also said in a Thursday post on X that he would leave after nearly five years at Maple. “I’ll be stepping down as COO. I’ve come to a different view on the direction Maple should take, and I’ve decided it’s time to step aside,” he wrote.

SYRUP traded at $0.12 at 10:36 p.m. UTC Thursday, down 7.5% over 24 hours and 12% over the past week, according to CoinGecko. The token had a market capitalization of about $145 million.

Maple and Powell did not respond to Cointelegraph’s requests for comment by publication.

In a statement published Wednesday, Maple confirmed that Flanagan was stepping down as chairman and leaving the company. “This is an agreed and orderly transition,” the company said, adding that his responsibilities would move to Powell and Maple’s existing leadership team.

The company did not announce a replacement chairman or specify how the departing executives’ duties would be carried out.

Flanagan said his differences with Powell reached a point where they were no longer constructive. “I am choosing to leave rather than continue supporting a direction I cannot stand behind,” he said. Flanagan added that he would help with the transition through the end of 2026.

O’Shea is stepping down effective Nov. 27. “I’ll have no ongoing role after that,” he wrote.

The departures come as Maple looks to expand beyond crypto-backed lending. In October, Powell said the firm planned to reach more customers through fintech partnerships and lend against a wider range of assets, including payments owed on loans made by fintech companies and securities backed by assets such as mortgages.

Related: Kraken, Maple launch onchain warehouse facility for crypto-backed institutional loans

The announcements come as Maple’s lending business continues to grow, while SYRUP is down 62% year to date and total value locked (TVL) has declined.

According to Token Terminal, Maple’s protocol revenue rose 8% year over year in October, while TVL fell around 11% between the end of September and Nov. 11.

Maple’s latest quarterly results also showed growth, with the company reporting $4.4 million in third-quarter revenue, up 5% from a year earlier. Assets under management rose 18% year over year to $4.7 billion.

Maple has also been using some of its revenue to buy back SYRUP tokens. In September, the company repurchased about 1.37 million tokens, twice as many as in August, according to its October update.

#5067. The 6 Best Undereye Patches, Tested and Reviewed by Dermatologists and Beauty Editors

The entire Women's Health team swears by them.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’m always up late doomscrolling TikTok and The White Lotus subreddit for season 4 theories. (AJ Michalka hive, stand up!) The only problem? Those late nights mean I have dark circles and puffiness in the morning (boo!). While I'm a huge fan of undereye creams, sometimes I get bored and need to switch things up. Enter undereye patches. They're a fast fix for dryness, puffiness, and dark circles—and even help me fake eight hours of sleep. "The skin under the eyes is prone to changes related to aging skin, such as fine lines, and conditions like dryness and discoloration," says dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD. In just 10 to 20 minutes, undereye patches temporarily hydrate the delicate skin and help me look refreshed. Plus, they're super cute and add a fun touch to my selfies, even if they're shared to just my Close Friends circle on Instagram Stories.

Like any other skin care product, eye masks really get their power from their ingredients, some of which are typically hyaluronic acid, vitamin C, niacinamide, and caffeine.

“Eye patches incorporate key ingredients like hyaluronic acid to boost moisture, peptides to firm, ceramides to strengthen the skin barrier, caffeine to help reduce puffiness, and niacinamide to reduce discoloration,” says dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD.

As with any beauty product, there are always a few things to consider before making the investment. Since these masks are mostly advertised for their ability to soothe and hydrate, you'll want to check the hydrating and firming ingredients, and keep your expectations realistic since results are usually temporary. Here's what to look out for.

For starters, look for key ingredients such as aloe, chamomile, cucumber, green tea, glycerin, or hyaluronic acid. You're less likely to come across vitamin C and retinol, but it's a plus if you do. Patches with a cellulose gel material can also prevent them from sliding off your face (a con I often deal with and try to avoid as much as possible).

Not only is the skin under your eyes thinner and more delicate than in other areas of your face, but it’s also where lymphatic fluid drainage occurs, says dermatologist Lauren Penzi, MD. It can also show more blood vessels, and in turn, make dark circles appear more visible, says Dr. Garshick. Most eye masks are created to reduce fine lines, undereye darkness, and wrinkles while giving your skin the boost of moisture it needs. The overall effect of these patches is to revive and hydrate, which is why so many people use them to get a more refreshed look.

Many people complain about looking tired, and eye patches are a nice, quick fix. Still, it's important to be realistic about the kind of results you'll get in just one or two uses. So, you’ll want to zero in on the reason you’re buying patches, says Dr. Camp. For example, you can target puffiness by rocking undereye patches infused with caffeine or green tea while getting ready for work, says Dr. Camp.

As a member of the beauty team at Women’s Health, I’m constantly on the hunt for the best products and spend a lot of my time testing and reviewing the latest drops. I frequently consult skin experts, which is exactly what I did to kick off my selection process here. I consulted five New York–based dermatologists and had them give their recommendations with insight on why these undereye masks are so splurge-worthy. Then, I tested several of their picks and compared them to some of the other undereye masks available in our beauty closet.To narrow down the list even further, I got a few other members of team WH, including Addison Aloian, Lily Wohlner, Brian Underwood, and Danielle Jackson, to get in on the testing process. Ingredients, price, and overall efficacy were taken into account to determine which would be best for a wide range of needs and preferences.Here are the fruits of our labor.

After testing tons of undereye masks, this one takes the cake for best overall. Why? It's the most hydrating option on this list and it doesn't slip off your face, which is super hard to find in an undereye mask.

ICYMI, Wander Beauty basically started the undereye mask trend. This OG mask is made with peptides, amino acids, and hyaluronic acid to improve your skin's texture, tone, and hydration. It's also expert-approved by Dr. Garshick and dermatologist Dendy Engelman, MD. "I love that this mask is made with three different layers that allow the formula to penetrate the skin deeply and prevent it from sliding off the face, so you can multitask while you wear it," says Dr. Engelman.

Wander Beauty patches are as effective as they are Instagrammable. I’ve been a fan of the rose gold and yellow gold patches for five years, and all of my beauty editor friends gush over them. They brighten, hydrate, and plump up my fine lines. They also contain calendula extract and aloe vera to help reduce puffiness. Ahem, hi holiday parties and upcoming travel—I’m looking at you.

These pretty patches have three unique layers: the surface's foil retains heat and prevents evaporation, the middle grips to prevent slippage, and the base delivers moisturizing glycerin and de-puffing calendula extract. For an extra soothing experience, I like to leave mine in the fridge. Cool temperatures help shrink blood vessels under the eyes, so dark circles appear lighter and puffiness minimizes, dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD, said in our guide to undereye skin care.

That said, the construction of this mask consists of super light and flexible material versus the conventional plastic material found in a lot of other eye patches that were tested, giving this product a high-quality feel.

I would be remiss if I didn't mention my personal fave patch from Patchology. It contains hyaluronic acid (hi, hydrated, plump skin) and feels super cool under the eyes to de-puff and smooth out that area.

Patchology is fantastic for targeting lines, says dermatologist Anar Mikailov, MD. He mentions that there's resveratrol, a natural antioxidant found in grapes that helps improve barrier function, and other antioxidants that provide protection against oxidizing agents that can visibly age the skin by causing wrinkles. There’s also antioxidant-rich strawberry extract, which helps brighten dark circles.

After using this patch, I also noticed my undereye area was less puffy and more luminous. My only con was that the mask slides out of place after a while, but it’s still epic to use and totally worth incorporating into your routine. My hack is to use these patches while lying down in bed to prevent any slipping.

This undereye mask is basically an expert at reducing puffy, tired-looking eyes thanks to its cooling effects. It also temporarily plumps up my fine lines with hydrating hyaluronic acid.

This option comes with a lot of serum, so it may slip down your face over time. But, feel free to go ahead and massage that extra serum into your undereye area—that little bit of massaging can help assist with lymphatic drainage and further reduce puffiness. Need even more convincing? Celebs like Jessica Alba post about this mask on her Instagram story time and time again, noting that she's a major fan.

Most masks on this list only need 10 minutes on the skin, but this one should stay on for up to 20. Although, 20 minutes fly by when you have a good book in hand (pro tip!).

These eye masks from Live Tinted are packed with copper peptides and banana extract (hi, Ashton Hall!) to reduce puffiness and smooth fine lines. They also reduce puffiness after just a few uses and leave skin looking glowy and feeling hydrated.

And because these patches help soften and smooth your delicate undereye area, Aloian relies on them for makeup prep. "Not only is the patch super cute—it's shaped like a sun—but it also genuinely hydrates and brightens my undereye area," she says. These patches make Aloian feel confident going makeup free because of the glow they leave behind, but it's just as helpful on days when she wants a dewy base before applying concealer.

Along with a mix of peptides to help stimulate collagen production, this eye mask contains niacinamide, bakuchiol, caffeine, and vitamin C. Bakuchiol is a great retinol alternative that helps stimulate collagen production, says Dr. Mikailov.

Wohlner also gave this patch a try and loves how flexible it is under the eye. However, she did note that it does tend to slip down the face because it's super thin.

This vitamin C-packed eye patch is perfect for helping brighten up the undereye area while reducing signs of aging and puffiness with the help of caffeine.

Yeah, it's a little pricier, but trust that it's totally worth it if you have the budget. The gel patches are super easy to apply. Plus, they can reduce discoloration and fine lines within just a few weeks. Sometimes I'm wary of products with vitamin C in them because the smell can be a bit aggressive, but these are just right.

Derms also deem this patch worth the money. "The key ingredient in this mask is THD Ascorbate Vitamin C, which is 50 times more powerful than other forms of vitamin C," says Dr. Engelman. THD is especially good for surface dark spots that need brightening rather than deeper dark circles, says Dr. Mikailov.

It's worth noting that these dry up around the 10-minute mark, and while they stay on really well, the edges break off easily if you try to move the masks around a few minutes after the initial application.

As the name suggests, this patch is meant to soothe tired-looking eyes. So, for those of you who have a lot of sleepless nights or are just night owls at heart, this is your winner. Infused with caffeine, niacinamide, and hyaluronic acid, these work overtime to reduce puffiness and dark circles.

"I often recommend Peace Out’s acne patch for the face, but I also love the brand’s eye patches," says Dr. Engelman. "It's so effective at quickly bringing down puffiness and brightening and smoothing the under-eyes." The patch is biodegradable and made with biocellulose, which helps the formula deeply penetrate the skin, says Dr. Engelman.

These patches fit snugly under my eyes, so I could wear them while doing my eye makeup. They also did a great job of catching eyeshadow fallout that would normally ruin my undereye concealer. Another pro? Unlike most gel patches, they weren’t completely soaked in serum, which can make the process a bit messy. Instead, they had just the right amount for ample hydration. After the initial use, I noticed my undereyes were softer and brighter, and I’d slowly reach for these patches for special occasions.

I’m not the only fan on WH’s beauty team. “I have very sensitive skin, so I'm always cautious when it comes to trying things out, but this didn't give me any issues,” says tester Sabrina Talbert. “It also doesn't have much of a scent, which put my mind at ease since fragrance tends to be an early indicator that my skin might not like a product.”

These patches are on the larger side, so they feel a bit bulky. They also need to be slightly adjusted because they slide down a little bit over 15 minutes, but honestly, they’re such minor cons that Talbert continues using them.

#5065. Lido’s lending plan could block loan repayments without stopping interest

The lending plan distinguishes a limited freeze from a broader pause that blocks repayments and lender withdrawals. Interest for the paused period can still be added once accounting resumes.

Under Lido Lend’s proposed emergency rules, borrowers could be blocked from paying down debt and lenders from withdrawing. When the pause ends, borrowers could owe more: the next successful interest update would count the time they spent locked out.

The distinction appears in Lido Lend’s November 9 consolidated proposal. The proposed lending protocol, built on a modified version of Morpho Blue, uses a controller contract to permit or reject market actions. It separates a limited market freeze from a broader controller pause. Only the second shuts down repayment, liquidation and lender settlement together. Lenders supply loan tokens that borrowers take out against pledged collateral.

The proposal reports that the core contracts are deployed on Ethereum mainnet, but the DAO would have to accept the protocol separately. Each market would then need its own motion or DAO vote. The forum discussion continued with a signer declaration on November 14; the thread did not announce a completed acceptance vote or creation of the first market.

A Guardian ban stops an account’s new borrowing and collateral maturation but does not itself stop repayment, liquidation, settlement or collateral withdrawal under the remaining rules. The expected first WETH/wstETH market would launch with one contributor-run Guardian and a 1-of-1 quorum, with independent Guardians intended later.

Under the market controller rules, a freeze stops new borrowing, new collateral from completing its activation delay, and collateral withdrawals from positions carrying debt. Repayment, liquidation, lender withdrawals and settlement remain available, subject to their ordinary checks.

The Risk Steward Committee could impose that freeze and tighten defined controller settings through its dashboard, but could not loosen them. The proposed Operational Committee would use bounded Easy Track motions, open to LDO-holder objections, for actions such as unfreezing.

Borrowers can pay down debt, a key consideration when comparing crypto loan terms. Lenders can withdraw available loan tokens or use eligible settlement, which reduces a lender’s claim and a borrower’s debt by the same amount in exchange for collateral valued by the protocol’s price feed.

Settlement is the mechanism behind the Fallback Exits CryptoSlate examined in October. Lenders can exit without available loan tokens, but settlement is subject to market rules and policy limits. Bad debt at the front of the borrower queue can block it.

An Exit Book, a system for posting withdrawal requests, has a separate pause that stops new withdrawal requests and fills in that book. Owners can still cancel requests or use underlying positions directly, but those routes cannot bypass a paused market controller.

A pause blocks those routes. The architecture specification says it stops actions subject to the controller, including repayment, lender withdrawals, liquidation, settlement and direct interest updates. Even a direct call to the core cannot bypass the pause. Vault-share transfers and core functions outside the controller’s scope remain available.

Blocking an interest-update call does not make the borrowing period free. The core accounting specification uses elapsed time to calculate interest, and the controller rules explicitly say a later successful accrual covers time since the last update. A borrower could therefore regain repayment access with a larger debt balance under the applicable interest-rate model.

Proposed controls differ in scope. A controller pause closes repayment and lender exits while elapsed-time interest still counts.

For the banned account, new borrowing and collateral maturation stop. Repayment, liquidation and lender exits remain subject to normal rules.

New borrowing, collateral maturation and debt-bearing collateral withdrawal stop. Repayment, liquidation and lender exits remain available under normal rules.

Repayment, liquidation and lender withdrawal or settlement are blocked, alongside other controller-checked actions. The interest clock is not stopped.

New requests and fills stop in the book. Cancellation and direct core or vault access remain subject to the underlying market’s controls.

A finite emergency power does not guarantee a finite interruption: a separate Reseal path can make an active pause indefinite.

Proposed Lido Lend design, not a live pause. Available routes remain subject to normal rules and other active controls. Interest depends on the IRM. Live market settings and permissions are not independently verified.

Source-bound permission and authority diagrams from the November 9 proposal and current specifications. Arrows identify affected action routes, not quantities or guaranteed execution. No numerical outcome chart is warranted.

Proposed Lido Lend design, not a live pause. Available routes remain subject to normal rules and other active controls. Interest depends on the IRM. Live market settings and permissions are not independently verified.

There is a protective reason to suspend more than new borrowing. The proposal warns that initial price feeds, or oracles, use issuer-published collateral rates, which may diverge from secondary-market prices. If collateral falls in the market without a corresponding rate change, liquidation may become uneconomic and settlement may deliver collateral worth less than the debt canceled. Pausing those transactions can contain that risk, while also interrupting borrowers trying to repay.

The proposed Lend Emergency Brakes Committee has a 3-of-6 signing threshold. Through CircuitBreaker, it could trigger one fixed-duration controller pause per registration while maintaining required liveness signals, called heartbeats. It could not select the duration, extend the pause or end it early.

The roles specification assigns duration configuration and pauser registration to a separate administrator within immutable bounds. The committee’s successful pause consumes its registration, so another use requires re-registration.

The repository’s mainnet profile selects a configuration with an initial pause of five minutes and a permitted range from one minute to 60 days. The first market’s actual setting has not been confirmed.

Automatic expiry also has an exception. The proposal says the protocol-wide Reseal Manager can make a pause indefinite when Dual Governance is outside its normal state. The published Reseal Manager and Dual Governance implementations require an active finite pause and an authorized Reseal Committee acting through the governance contract. That path can replace the finite pause with an indefinite one without a fresh ordinary DAO vote at that step.

These controls apply per Lido Lend market and do not themselves move user assets. Separate DAO-controlled proxy upgrades remain part of the protocol’s trust assumptions.

For the first WETH/wstETH market, watch for the configured pause duration and who can extend it indefinitely. Those decisions will determine how long borrowers could be stuck with an interest bill they cannot stop by repaying.

#5064. This New AI Music Model Is Already Better Than Suno—We Put ACE to the Test

This New AI Music Model Is Already Better Than Suno—We Put ACE to the Test

Artificial intelligence has gotten pretty good at writing songs. Now, a relatively unfamiliar competitor has managed to beat Suno, arguably the biggest name in AI music, at its own game.

ACE Music v1, developed by ACE Studio, has taken first place on Artificial Analysis' vocal music leaderboard, scoring 1,160 Elo points against Suno v6's 1,144.

The AA-Music-Vocal v1.1 benchmark measures the quality of AI-generated songs containing vocals. Evaluators listen to tracks produced from identical prompts without knowing which model created them, then choose their favorite. Those preferences determine an Elo-style rating, with higher scores indicating stronger listener preference.

The lead is relatively narrow, and the models' statistical confidence intervals overlap. Suno also retains the top position on the separate instrumental music leaderboard.

ACE Studio, founded in 2018, originally focused on synthesizing singing voices from MIDI notes and lyrics. Its latest ACE Music v1 model generates complete songs from written descriptions or user-provided lyrics.

In Decrypt's hands-on tests, ACE Music consistently produced more melodic and coherent songs in mainstream styles.

That said, the vocal performances sounded more natural in general, with fewer of the synthetic artifacts that sometimes make AI singers sound like they're struggling to pronounce their own lyrics, use a lot of autotune or hallucinate words just to fill spaces. (Go ahead and give our song a listen here, which incidentally is about our latest company announcement regarding the Information Exchange.)

ACE also handled song endings better. Where Suno occasionally introduces strange sounds, unnecessary repetitions, hallucinations or abrupt musical changes near the finish, ACE generally maintained its structure and delivered cleaner conclusions.

That matters because making a convincing chorus is relatively easy compared with maintaining a musical idea throughout an entire composition even if the lyrics are already over.

Suno still had an advantage when we pushed the models toward less conventional genres.

In our melodic death metal test, ACE consistently produced tracks featuring a woman singing clearly in a pleasant, clean voice, missing the aggressive vocal delivery expected from the requested style. In general it confuses metal genres all over. Suno offered more creative arrangements in the proper heavy styles, with better stylistic consistency in several similarly demanding prompts.

The results were subjective rather than a controlled benchmark, but they showed why a leaderboard victory doesn't automatically make one model better for every musician.

ACE's most interesting feature may be its songwriting workflow.

Its “Idea” feature can develop a basic concept into lyrics and a structured composition, identifying individual song sections and describing how they should be arranged. Users can then refine the material rather than repeatedly generating completely new tracks.

The v1.1 Preview goes further, creating a musical score before generating audio.

“Each generation is a new performance, so the sound may differ even when the score stays the same,” the developers explain.

Users can edit melodies and chords, regenerate performances, export MIDI files and separate vocals from instruments for further production.

That workflow puts ACE closer to a music production assistant than a simple prompt-to-song application.

The flagship ACE Music v1 model remains closed-source with no public API, so users can only generate via the official site. However, its developers are pursuing a parallel open-source strategy.

ACE Studio and StepFun have already released ACE-Step 1.5, a separate family of models whose code and weights are publicly available. Unlike the proprietary flagship, these can run on users' own hardware—but using a weaker model.

The company also promises another release.

“We plan to open-source ACE Music v1 Flash in late 2026,” the developers state on their website, describing a version designed to balance quality, generation speed and hardware requirements.

ACE Music is available through its browser application, with a limited free tier and paid subscriptions. Commercial usage rights for flagship-model songs require a paid plan, while ACE-Step offers a separate free generation option.

For now, ACE Music v1 holds a 16-point Elo lead over Suno v6 in vocal generation. Its promised Flash release would give local users another model to try before the end of 2026.

#5062. 10 Best Moisturizers for Mature Skin in 2026, According to Dermatologists

Our favorites include Olay, Neutrogena, and Avène.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As you age, your face shows signs of wrinkles, sun damage, and dryness. Getting older is totally normal and, frankly, should be celebrated. Your beautiful expression lines are earned and represent wisdom and happy memories over the years. Dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD, says a gentle cleanser, a moisturizer for mature skin, and sunscreen can keep your skin looking healthy with age.

With fall here, it’s essential to slather on a moisturizer tailored to your skin type and concerns, like perimenopausal acne, a common beauty change for women in their 40s. Face creams and lotions relieve dryness, maintain hydration, and support your skin barrier, says Dr. Camp.

These dermatologist-recommended moisturizers also help prevent your makeup from settling, flaking, and pilling. In just a few weeks, you might need less foundation and concealer because your natural skin becomes a smoother, glowing base. Talk about skincare goals.

There are so many face moisturizers for mature skin available. Amazon has 100 bestsellers alone. Some are geared toward skin types, including dry or acne-prone complexions, while others are more ingredient-focused. That’s where the Women’s Health beauty team comes into play. We’re here to assist with a quick breakdown of how to buy moisturizers for mature skin, according to dermatologists.

First, think about your main skincare concerns and let them guide your shopping.

Are you looking to plump up fine lines and wrinkles? Retinoids, like retinol and retinal, are vitamin A derivatives that promote skin cell turnover, boost collagen and elastin, and minimize discoloration, dermatologist Hadley King, MD, recently told WH in our guide to wrinkle creams. Plus, retinol helps improve the appearance of crepey skin by boosting collagen production and improving the firmness of skin, says Dr. Camp.

Speaking of collagen, your skin naturally loses it and elastin as you age, so slathering on a collagen-supporting moisturizer is helpful. With regular use, you’ll notice a firmer complexion.

If age spots and hyperpigmentation have you down, then choose moisturizers made with brightening ingredients, like vitamin C, niacinamide, and azelaic acid. Glycolic acid, which is naturally found in sugarcane, beets, and pineapple, earned snaps from dermatologist Richard Bottiglione, MD. It’s an alpha hydroxy acid (AHA) that boasts the smallest molecule size, meaning your skin absorbs it easily for quicker results. Notably, it increases collagen production for a smoothing and plumping effect.

Hormonal changes and reduced sebum production make mature skin prone to dryness, says Dr. Camp. He suggests products that improve the skin's barrier function and retain hydration. My favorite is the viral Avène Cicalfate+ Restorative Protective Cream. Your skin will soak up hyaluronic acid moisturizers like a tall glass of water. He’s also keen on ceramides, glycerin, and squalane for moisturizing. Dr. Camp prefers intensely hydrating creams that target fine lines, wrinkles, and dark spots. We’ve got you covered with dermatologist-recommended, editor-tested solutions in this guide.

Forget the myth that face moisturizers for mature skin must be thick and heavy. According to Dr. Camp, the best one for you depends on the formulation.

We’ve covered moisturizers for mature skin since 2021. For our October 2026 update, our beauty team went beyond simple research to find the best moisturizers for mature skin. We began by interviewing four board-certified dermatologists to determine the no-fail ingredients, formulations, and moisturizers that deliver anti-aging and hydrating benefits.

Their suggestions were a starting point for our team—WH beauty director Brian Underwood and me, Nicole Saunders—to test IRL. Together, we bring over 30 years of experience in beauty journalism and hands-on product testing to this guide.

We reevaluated old standbys to ensure they still outperformed the latest drops from 2026. Over the past year, we tested 37 products and narrowed them down to the 10 best moisturizers for mature skin actually worth buying.

Testing 37 picks over an entire year allowed us to closely monitor how each face moisturizer applied and how our results evolved. We evaluated their compatibility with various skin types and carefully compared how our results evolved from first impressions to several months of daily use. A few questions we considered include:

During the chilly fall and winter, we checked whether rich face creams left our skin supple and soft. Think gentle, nourishing, and thick formulations that we rely on during retinol recovery nights and during ski trips. We also included lightweight lotions that don’t leave our skin greasy by lunchtime for upcoming warm-weather winter destinations.

We tested each moisturizer's performance in different climates, ranging from cool New York falls to trips to the Caribbean. Airplane cabins are notoriously dry, so we also paid attention to how long each hydration level lasts for us while flying. We also wanted to ensure each container didn’t accidentally spill in our toiletry bags—a beauty struggle I know all too well.

Confession time: I’m a beauty editor, and I don’t have perfect skin. Since I’m testing an endless number of skincare products, my face is bound to react. It’s a minor occupational hazard, but one I don’t totally mind to deliver you the most honest product feedback possible.

In addition to their key ingredients and texture, we carefully evaluated their compatibility with various skin types, their performance with wrinkles, dryness, and spots, and how well they layered underneath makeup and sunscreen. We eliminated creams that pilled—when moisturizers don’t absorb and turn into tiny flakes or rolled-up balls—when paired with our other favorite beauty products.

In our guide to the best skincare products for your 40s, Dr. Camp and fellow dermatologist Dara Spearman, MD, said that you don’t always have to splurge on products to see results. “A well-formulated drugstore product can work as effectively as luxury creams if it has the right ingredients and consistency,” Dr. Camp said. We included some drugstore options from Olay and Neutrogena that won’t strain your budget.

Lastly, we also factored in each moisturizer's consistency, smell, and price to help determine its overall value. Ultimately, these are the best moisturizers for mature skin that we'll continue using because they're really worth our hard-earned coins.

A dashboard shared by trader Flood estimates an unrealized loss of about $9 billion, but applies August purchase costs to November holdings.

Trader Flood, who posts as @ThinkingUSD, called Ethereum a “contender for the worst asset of all time” on Nov. 13, sharing a dashboard that put BitMine’s unrealized loss at about $9 billion.

The image marked the Ethereum treasury company 43% underwater. Its holdings match BitMine’s November disclosure, while its average-cost field is dated August. Applying that older average to the later balance approximately reproduces the dashboard’s displayed cost, leaving its loss figure dependent on that assumption.

Flood cited money lost to hacks, development time spent on inadequate tools and retail losses from betting on Ethereum’s price. He supplied no figures for those categories or comparative data establishing an all-time ranking. His criticism targeted Ethereum, with the BitMine dashboard providing a specific example of treasury exposure.

The image Flood shared listed 6,070,092 ETH, a $3,380 average cost, a $20.52 billion total cost basis and an $11.69 billion market value. Its displayed unrealized loss was $8,829,920,029.

The average-cost field is labeled as the filed average for Aug. 31, 2026. BitMine’s annual accounts reported 5,901,837 ETH at that date, with a cost basis of about $19.95 billion and a fair value of about $14.56 billion. Dividing the cost by the quantity gives approximately $3,380 per ETH.

Those accounts were filed on Nov. 10, but the holdings and cost figures describe the August balance.

BitMine’s Nov. 9 release reported a larger holding of 6,070,092 ETH as of Nov. 8 at 2 p.m. ET. Multiplying that quantity by the rounded August average produces roughly the $20.52 billion cost basis displayed on Flood’s dashboard.

That calculation extrapolates across two reporting dates. It reproduces the rounded total without confirming the dashboard’s underlying methodology or establishing what the expanded ETH holding actually cost. The November release supplies no updated aggregate cost basis.

The dashboard’s $8.83 billion loss estimate is therefore an unrealized mark against an assumed cost. It provides no evidence that BitMine sold those holdings and realized the loss in cash.

#5060. Gemini’s quarterly retail trading volume sinks to 3-year low

Gemini’s third-quarter trading rebound masked a deepening retail slump.

Crypto exchange Gemini has just reported its lowest quarterly retail trading volume in three years, despite an increase in overall crypto trading volume.

Total spot trading volume rose 18% from the second quarter to $4.5 billion, according to Gemini’s Q3 earnings report. Institutional volume climbed 26% to $3.9 billion, while retail volume fell 14% to $600 million, its lowest level since the third quarter of 2023.

Gemini said the quarterly increase in spot trading volume was “supported by increased institutional Zcash activity and expanded affiliated market-making,” but did not give a specific reason for the decline in retail trading.

Despite the retail slump, Gemini’s exchange revenue increased 7% from the previous quarter to $13.4 million as institutional revenue more than doubled. Retail traders remained its largest source of exchange revenue, contributing nearly three-quarters of the total.

A number of crypto exchanges also reported softer crypto trading activity in the most recent quarter.

Coinbase reported softer retail and institutional activity, with consumer spot trading volume falling 9% from the previous quarter to $23.4 billion. Coinbase chief financial officer Alesia Haas said “continued growth in prediction markets helped offset softer crypto trading activity.”

At Robinhood, crypto revenue fell 55% year-on-year to $120 million, offset by a sixfold increase in event-contract revenue to $173 million.

Related: Strategy stock sheds 5% amid MSCI index removal, Bitcoin sell-off

Gemini also got some help from its own prediction exchange, Gemini Predictions, with revenue from that business unit increasing 52% quarter-on-quarter to $796,000, though it wasn’t significant enough to offset declines elsewhere.

Gemini reported stronger prediction-market activity heading into the fourth quarter, with average daily traders in October running about 50% above the third-quarter average.

Nearly a third of new prediction traders were new to Gemini, more than double the proportion in Q3.

The company is also seeking to distribute its event contracts through other platforms. An August nonbinding agreement with Apex Fintech Solutions would make Gemini Titan the exclusive venue for crypto event contracts distributed through Apex’s futures brokerage to its brokerage customers, subject to definitive agreements.

Gemini is set to host a Q3 earnings call on Friday.

#5058. Bitcoin Short-Term Holders Send $3.6 Billion in BTC to Exchanges at a Loss

Bitcoin Short-Term Holders Send $3.6 Billion in BTC to Exchanges at a Loss

Bitcoin investors who bought recently are moving tens of thousands of coins to cryptocurrency exchanges at a loss, adding to concerns about selling pressure as the cryptocurrency falls toward the low-$70,000 range.

CryptoQuant’s latest short-term holder profit-and-loss chart shows roughly 47,300 BTC transferred to exchanges below their acquisition price over 24 hours, compared with only about 1,100 BTC arriving at a profit.

Combined inflows stood near 48,500 BTC, or around $3.6 billion at Bitcoin’s current price of approximately $74,000.

The research company's chart below shows transfers, not completed sales. Sending Bitcoin to an exchange can be the first step toward selling, but some deposits are made for trading for other tokens, collateral, or other services. The data also does not establish exactly how much of the transferred Bitcoin was subsequently sold.

The distinction is important because the chart measures the behavior of short-term holders, a group that CryptoQuant generally defines as investors holding Bitcoin for less than 155 days.

These are often the buyers most exposed to a sudden price reversal, particularly when their holdings are worth less than they paid.

In a November 11 CryptoQuant analysis, contributor Amr Taha identified two large waves of underwater exchange deposits over the previous week: 50,790 BTC on November 3 and 46,060 BTC on November 10.

“On November 10, profitable transfers stood near 1,700 BTC, meaning approximately 27 BTC arrived at a loss for every 1 BTC transferred at a profit,” Taha wrote.

That is an unusually one-sided flow. Investors moving coins into exchanges are overwhelmingly doing so at prices below those at which they acquired them, rather than cashing in gains from the earlier rally.

A similar pattern has occurred over several months, with recurring spikes in loss-making exchange transfers as Bitcoin’s price swung higher and lower. The latest red spike appears near the deepest readings visible since July.

A separate CryptoQuant chart breaks down deposits to Binance by the time since each Bitcoin last moved on-chain. It shows 3,290 BTC arriving from coins last moved one day to one week earlier on November 1, followed by a much larger 8,114 BTC from the same category on November 3.

On November 9, the platform also received 1,925 BTC from coins last moved one to three months earlier, according to Taha’s analysis. Those figures help identify which age groups are active, but they do not necessarily reveal when the owners originally purchased their Bitcoin.

The Binance chart measures one exchange and groups coins by their last on-chain movement. The profit-and-loss charts track short-term holders sending coins to exchanges more broadly.

The timing matters because Bitcoin has been sliding from its late-September highs above $85,000 into the $73,000-to-$74,000 area visible at the end of the screenshots. A newer buyer who paid $80,000 would be sitting on a paper loss of roughly 7.5% with Bitcoin at $74,000; selling at that price would lock it in.

The recent weakness is not limited to short-term holders. Glassnode identified about 4 million BTC held by longer-term investors that had been acquired between $85,000 and $118,000, potentially leaving another pocket of underwater supply above current prices.

#5056. The Fed could rescue bond markets and still make life harder for Bitcoin

Lorie Logan wants emergency support for Treasury markets while favoring further rate hikes, leaving Bitcoin exposed to tighter monetary policy.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan proposed stronger tools to keep Treasury markets functioning during a crisis while leaving room for higher interest rates. Her November 13 remarks separate two potential influences on Bitcoin: relief from disrupted funding and pressure from further monetary tightening.

In the speech, Logan said the Treasury market was functioning very well and presented personal recommendations, rather than announcing an intervention or an adopted Federal Open Market Committee program. She said intervention should be reserved for extreme failures in intermediation; high or rapidly rising yields alone would not justify it.

Her rate outlook points toward further tightening. In November 10 remarks, Logan described current monetary policy as accommodative and called for at least two further quarter-point increases to make it modestly restrictive. She made the pace conditional on developments. The FOMC's October 28 decision had maintained the target range at 3.75% to 4%; her preferred path is distinct from that committee decision.

Her preferred starting point is lending against Treasury securities. The Fed could supply funding at a rate consistent with its monetary-policy target, supporting financial stability while maintaining the interest-rate stance it considers necessary.

Logan also proposed developing central clearing for the Fed's repo lending. Reducing the balance-sheet costs intermediaries incur when passing funding onward could help that money reach the broader market more efficiently during stress.

Purchases would serve a different need. When lending cannot resolve dysfunction, buying securities could free space on intermediaries' balance sheets so they can keep trading. But purchases are harder to separate from monetary policy because they can push down term premiums and stimulate the economy.

Logan suggested holding market-function purchases in a separate account and committing to sell the securities as soon as possible. She argued that purchases expected to unwind quickly should have much less effect on term premiums than holdings kept for years. That would limit the unwanted stimulus, rather than guarantee its elimination.

Logan's Nov. 13 proposals separate market repair from monetary easing; her Nov. 10 rate outlook calls for more tightening. She says Treasury trading is functioning well. No rescue was announced.

Funding relief could support risk-taking while further tightening could still weigh on Bitcoin.

For Bitcoin, the implication is conditional. Restoring disrupted Treasury funding could improve the environment for risk-taking. Yet further monetary tightening could still weigh on crypto risk appetite, even if the financial system were functioning more smoothly.

An August 2023 IMF working paper supplies historical evidence for that second channel. It finds that US monetary tightening reduces a common crypto price factor through risk-taking, resembling the transmission to equities. That aggregate finding is not a forecast of Bitcoin's response to Logan's proposals.

#5054. The 7 Best Microcurrent Devices of 2026 Tested by Women’s Health Editors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

We’re living in the golden age of high-tech skincare devices—and as our beauty editor, I couldn’t be happier. Red light therapy devices, including LED face masks, provide excellent anti-aging benefits from the comfort of our couch, while face steamers have replaced my need for pricey spa facials. Laser hair removal devices are becoming more inclusive by offering technology safe enough for deeper complexions. Face massagers also help de-puff skin after a hangover. However, when it comes to lifting saggy skin, microcurrent devices are the ultimate MVP skincare tool deserving of a spot in your beauty arsenal.

Think of them as a sculpting workout for your face without the sweat. “Microcurrent devices use low levels of electrical current to stimulate facial muscles, helping to boost collagen and sculpt and lift the face,” says dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD. And don’t worry: These aren’t painful. You’ll notice more of a temporary tingling sensation that’ll disappear within minutes of using the device.

While these at-home machines aren’t as powerful as the ones used by professionals, they’re a more cost-effective option for achieving subtle improvements, says dermatologist Bradley Glodny, MD. You’ll just need some patience to find a weekly cadence and intensity level that works for you. (More on that in a bit.) And if you’re getting seasonal in-office microcurrent treatments, these at-home machines help enhance and sustain your professional results over time, says Dr. Garshick.

What was once a closely guarded secret among my fellow beauty editors and plastic surgeons has now become increasingly popular and readily accessible across our most trusted sites, such as Sephora, Ulta, and Amazon. But an influx of hundreds of options can be overwhelming, which is where I come in. My years of reporting and research have informed this shopping guide. I also consulted the pros about what to look out for when buying at-home microcurrent machines. Ahead are a few non-negotiables to keep in mind, which helped inform the devices we tested and ultimately featured in this story.

Most devices on this list have a range of microcurrent levels—some, like Foreo, even go up to 10. The higher you go, the more intense the microcurrent will feel. If you're accustomed to microcurrent and prefer a device with more power and customization options, opt for one that offers multiple microcurrent levels.

On the other hand, if you're a beginner, you might only need to purchase a device with a few microcurrent levels, such as the NuFace Trinity.

Dr. Garshick advises using your microcurrent device at least three times a week for four to six weeks before you can expect to see results, although some devices recommend daily use. “While much of the initial benefit may only be noticed for hours to days, with consistent use, the results will continue as collagen production can take six or more months,” she says.

After the initial treatment period, you can decrease the frequency of treatments to two to three times per week to maintain your results. Always refer to the specific instructions for use of your microcurrent device.

Many microcurrent devices come with additional features, such as interchangeable attachments, smartphone app connectivity, and even instructional guides.

An added bonus for your microcurrent device is FDA approval, which means that the government organization has determined that the device is safe and effective for its intended use. This is not a necessity when purchasing a microcurrent device, but it's definitely a solid addition if you're looking for something that has been rigorously tested.

You’ll also want to order a microcurrent device that either includes a priming gel or purchase one separately. They’re conductive and allow the electrical currents to be transmitted from the device to the skin. They also help the device glide easily across the skin and help prevent irritation.

Unlike bulky in-office machines, at-home microcurrent devices are about the size of a closed fist. Someone who travels often might prefer the Solawave Facial Wand, a slim option that resembles a T-shaped salad fork. Regardless of which of these featured options you order, they won’t take up too much space in your medicine cabinet or cosmetic bag.

At-home microcurrent machines aren’t exactly cheap. Entry-level models cost around $150, while high-end options can easily go for upwards of $500. However, you’ll save money over time because you get multiple uses out of a single device. And if it helps ease the burden, I spent $275 for a pro microcurrent facial, which costs $60 more than the WH Skincare Award-winning Laduora Lumeo and conductive gel.

With the above dermatological guidance in mind, I began whittling down our list of contenders. The Women’s Health beauty closet was my first stop, along with my at-home collection of skincare devices. Of course, because I’m inquisitive and love knowing what the pros actually use IRL and recommend to their patients, I asked both Dr. Garshick and Dr. Glodny for their fail-safe picks. I eliminated anything that was cumbersome. For example, anything with a short cord or an extra-long one that easily tangled was cut. Were the cordless devices easy to charge quickly if I was in a crunch? Were there any other buttons or features that are easy to accidentally hit while rolling the device across my face?

These aren’t exactly short treatments. We’ll need at least a few minutes per treatment session, so caring for an entire face can easily take 15 minutes or more. I prioritized lightweight, but durable devices that easily slide across my skin. Anything that made my wrist tired after a few minutes was docked points. Was the tingling too intense for beginners or best suited for novices? Are there enough levels for both beginners and experienced users?

This NuFace device ticks all the boxes on my microcurrent wish list. The lifting effect smoothens the appearance of wrinkles and contours my cheekbones and jawline, even without makeup. #5053. Stablecoin Drain, ETF Outflows Leave Bitcoin 'Running on Empty'

Stablecoin Drain, ETF Outflows Leave Bitcoin 'Running on Empty'

The pool of dollars that fuels crypto trading is draining.

Total stablecoin supply fell by $14.2 billion over the 30 days through Nov. 9, the fastest contraction since June 2022, according to a report published Wednesday by onchain analytics firm Glassnode.

The total stablecoin supply now sits just below $280 billion, and the research company suggests that's a big reason why Bitcoin is currently "running on empty."

Stablecoins, tokens typically pegged to the U.S. dollar, serve as crypto’s cash. Traders park money in them on exchanges and onchain before buying other assets.

When the stablecoin supply shrinks, it means holders are redeeming tokens for dollars and pulling that money out of crypto entirely, which Glassnode said leaves “less fuel for a rally.” The firm said a return to supply growth would be the first sign that fresh money is coming in.

The stablecoin drain isn’t the only sign of money leaving. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.6 billion in net redemptions over 20 trading sessions, the report found, and Bitcoin has traded at a discount on Coinbase, a gauge of U.S. demand.

Bitcoin also slipped below the average cost basis of short-term holders, about $75,600, leaving most recent buyers underwater, and traded near $73,000 on Wednesday. Over $3.6 billion in Bitcoin was recently moved over to exchanges, potentially to be sold, at a loss, according to a separate report from CryptoQuant today.

Glassnode did point to some silver linings. The slide has flushed out most leveraged long positions near the current price, buy orders outweigh sell orders in the order book, and wallets holding between 100 and 10,000 BTC have started accumulating.

The firm flagged $73,000 as key support and said the broader trend change that began in August remains intact as long as Bitcoin holds above its June low.

The contraction comes as stablecoins face growing competition from traditional finance.

Global banks including Goldman Sachs, Citi, and Deutsche Bank are backing a $270 million challenge to crypto’s dominant stablecoin issuers, and the Federal Reserve recently unveiled stablecoin rules on reserves and capital.

#5049. The 10 Best Red Light Therapy Tools of 2026, Tested by Beauty Experts

Our top picks—from Omnilux, TheraFace, and Qure—treat acne, boost collagen, and more.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you're starting to notice that your skin is looking a little, well, tired, you're not alone. The visible signs of aging—I’m talking fine lines and wrinkles, dullness, even sallow skin—will strike us all sooner or later. Bummer. On the bright side, we're living in an age when there's no shortage of smart beauty devices and skincare products for these issues. From wrinkle-smoothing injections like Botox and fillers to anti-aging creams, you've got an arsenal of skin-boosting tools at your disposal.

But what if I were to tell you that there's one such solution that takes roughly 10 a day and can be done while you're relaxing in bed scrolling TikTok? Enter red light therapy.

Red light therapy has exploded in popularity lately because it's convenient, noninvasive, and can be done at home. It uses a specific spectrum of visible light that offers a host of beauty benefits—low-level laser light therapy can effectively treat scars, vitiligo, and psoriasis, research shows. It has an anti-inflammatory effect and can even help to smooth wrinkles, too. So, how does it work? We know that red light penetrates 2 to 3 millimeters into skin's dermis, where it's “absorbed by light-sensitive porphyrins in the mitochondria of skin cells, stimulating energy production in fibroblasts to churn out more collagen,” says dermatologist Ava Shamban, MD.

But the goodness doesn't stop there. Red light can also help fade dark spots and manage eczema, plus boost hair growth, says dermatologist Purvisha Patel, MD. These at-home devices can be expensive, but they're an investment you can use for a years to come: Many red light therapy tools are also equipped with blue lights, which are particularly effective at treating acne (say buh-bye to those period or menopausal breakouts) and other concerns. Bottom line: At any age—and for years to come—these red light therapy tools can be a beneficial addition to your beauty routine.

Ultimately, these are the devices that we’ll continue to use and would genuinely repurchase if we had to start our skincare routine from scratch. The best part? Our faves start at just $72, which is a major win for a category that easily ranges from $300 to $700.

I've got a great list of options for you, but if you find yourself in the market for a red light therapy tool, here are a few things to keep in mind.

There are several kinds of red light therapy devices to choose from, including panels, masks, and facial wands, and one may be a better fit for you based on your lifestyle and the area you're seeking to treat.

LED masks are the most common variety you'll find for home use because most are hands-free and contain a lot of diodes (a fancy way of referring to the individual lightbulbs), offering a powerful burst of light to treat the face, neck, or chest.

Maybe you're claustrophobic and the idea of wearing masks gives you the heebie-jeebies—that's where panels come in. They look like flexible bodyboards that you lie down under, and they come in a diverse range of shapes and sizes, each offering different levels of red light exposure to your face, décolletage, and back. These also help replace the need for a separate lip-specific red light therapy tool.

Wands are appealing when you want to target smaller specific areas (the crow's feet or smile lines, for example) and prefer to do your treatments on the go (you can walk around while using these).

Our eyes are the first place to show signs of aging, so you’ll want to take a cue from dermatologist Pooja Rambhia, MD, and use these affordable red light therapy eye tools. Red, deep red, and near-infrared wavelengths target fine lines, wrinkles, darkness, and puffiness early on, making them a smart preventive beauty move.

It's tempting to pick a device with the quickest treatment window, especially if you don't have loads of free time to sit back and chill with a red light mask. But remember: To treat more advanced signs of aging, a longer treatment time may be more beneficial. Look at the full picture before you base your purchase on the convenience of a quicker treatment. And for what it’s worth, almost all of our featured recommendations can be used in just three minutes, so even busy women can incorporate quick treatments into their routine.

You may notice the abbreviation nm on the outer packaging of many of these tools. This stands for nanometers and refers to the wavelength of the light that the device emits—an important metric to consider, says dermatologist Jody A. Levine, MD. "Red light typically falls between 630 and 660 nanometers, and is good for targeting fine lines and mild discoloration," says Dr. Levine. If you're looking for something slightly more powerful—to deal with deeper wrinkles, sagging, or stubborn pigmentary problems—go with a device that cranks up to the near-infrared range (between 800 and 850 nanometers) to penetrate deeper.

Our beauty team is well-versed in red light therapy tools. We’ve been updating this story since December 2022—and I’ve been writing about these devices since November 2019. I've also been using red light therapy tools since April 2018. They've significantly diminished my stubborn fine lines and hyperpigmentation—and when I stop for a few months, they slowly reappear.
